newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Thais run first major evacuation from Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Thais run first major evacuation from Cambodia.

text.p: Hundreds of foreigners ran across the tarmac and scrambled into Thai military transport planes at Phnom Penh's battered airport on Tuesday, fleeing the Cambodian capital after three days of fighting and turmoil.

In a scene reminiscent of the evacuation of Phnom Penh just before Khmer Rouge guerrillas seized the city in 1975, the frightened foreigners boarded three Thai airforce C-130 planes to escape the war-torn city.
"I've got to get my wife and children out of here," said American Gary Jahn, an agriculture aid worker who was leaving the country with his Thai wife and their two young children.
Jahn said shells had landed near his Phnom Penh home during the fighting on Saturday and Sunday.
Thai air force commandos who arrived on the aircraft formed a perimeter around the planes as people ran towards them to try to flee the city.
The first plane took off for Thailand at about 0335 GMT, and by about 0400 GMT a total of three aircraft had departed.

A Thai official organising the evacuation said the planes should each make at least one more trip on Tuesday, making for a total of six flights. Officials hoped to take up to 700 people out of the country.

Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said in Bangkok on Tuesday that apart from more than 700 Thai citizens, some 120 Americans, 100 New Zealanders and 300 Pakistanis had also requested to be taken out in the airplanes.
He said the first priority was to the Thais but they would try and help others.
The Thai ambassador in Phnom Penh, Domedej Bunnag, safd today's evacuation of Thai natioanls was "definitely the biggest in two decades".

He added that the Netherlands had also requsted help in evacuating its nationals. He said Thailand was likely to able to help in evacuating foreign nationals tomorrow but this depended on the continuing improvement in the situation and getting necessary logicstics in place.

Phnom Penh's airport, closed since Saturday, was a scene of utter devastation after the weekend's fighting and extensive looting on Monday. It was stripped of all equipment and ransacked over the three days of violence in the capital and its surroundings.
"I am absolutely happy to get out," said Punnika Srisuanthanch, who was leaving for Bangkok with her 17 year old daughter.

The Thais were crammed into mini-busses and pickup trucks and driven through areas which experienced heavy fighting at the weekend. Burned-out tanks and charred factories lined the main road from the city centre to the airport.

Not everyone waiting at the airport was able to get on the first flights. Among those left behind on the tarmac and hoping to get on a later flight was Somchai Varvilay who said he was delighted to be leaving.
"This city is very dangerous," said Somchai, holding his two-year old son. "I have to save my family; it's barbaric here."
